metadata.title: CoconutEval | The pitch
metadata.description: A six-slide visual introduction to function classification, optimization, and the conditions agents must preserve.

slides.title: CoconutEval.
slides.introduction:
How well does a language model understand
the shape of a function?

graph.accessibilityLabel: The convex curve y equals x squared, with a chord above the curve

slides.instruction: Classify the function as convex, concave, or neither on the given interval.

slides.title: Convex, concave, or neither.
slides.introduction: All three functions use the interval D = [−1, 1].

graph.accessibilityLabel: Graph of x squared on [−1, 1]. The curve lies below the dashed chord joining (−1, 1) and (1, 1).

cards.title: Concave

graph.accessibilityLabel: Graph of minus x squared on [−1, 1]. The curve lies above the dashed chord joining (−1, −1) and (1, −1).

cards.explanation: Curves downward like an upside-down cup (∩).

cards.title: Neither

graph.accessibilityLabel: Graph of x cubed on [−1, 1]. The curve lies above the chord from (−1, −1) to (0, 0), violating convexity, and below the chord from (0, 0) to (1, 1), violating concavity.

cards.explanation: Some chords lie above the graph; others lie below it.
cards.definition: Neither convex nor concave on D.

slides.chordExplanation: A chord joins two graph points with a straight segment. For f: D → ℝ, any x, y ∈ D and t ∈ [0, 1], set z = tx + (1 − t)y.
notes: Each inequality must hold for every x, y and t above.
Affine functions satisfy both; this evaluation excludes them.

slides.title:
Check the objective
and the constraints.

cards.title: Optimal control

graph.accessibilityLabel: Control loop: state determines an action, producing a next state that is compared with a target.

cards.description: Check whether a control cost and its constraints form a convex problem.

cards.title: Inverse problems

graph.accessibilityLabel: Inverse problem: observed data enters an objective combining a fit term and a regularizer to produce an estimate.

cards.description: Check whether adding a regularizer keeps a data-fitting objective convex.

cards.title: Resource allocation

graph.accessibilityLabel: Resource allocation: one fixed total capacity is divided among three demands.

cards.description: Check costs and capacity constraints before choosing a convex solver.

slides.caveat: CoconutEval measures scalar function classification. These applications are illustrative; transfer to full optimization systems remains untested.

slides.title: Check the whole rule.

cards.title: Travel planner
cards.request: Find a cheaper flight to Delhi that arrives before 6 pm.
cards.arrival: Arrives at 5 pm, before the deadline

outcome.title: Reject this route
outcome.explanation: The arrival works. The connection breaks the rule.

cards.title: Customer support
cards.request: An opened item reportedly arrived damaged. The refund request comes on day 12.

outcome.title: Check the damage exception
outcome.explanation: Opening the box alone is not a reason to reject.

cards.title: Coding agent
cards.request: Let managers export invoices alongside admins. Both roles must belong to the invoice’s workspace.

outcome.title: Keep the workspace check
outcome.explanation: A separate “or manager” could let someone from another workspace export invoices.

slides.caveat: These examples explain why conditions matter. We have not tested whether CoconutEval scores predict success in these agent workflows.

steps.title: Verify the reference answer
steps.description: Generate a function and interval. Verify its label before adding it to the evaluation.

steps.title: Ask the model
steps.description: Send the expression and interval in three fresh requests. Keep the reference answer and proof out of the prompt.

steps.title: Score and inspect the answers
steps.description: Report macro-F1 and each class’s recall. Track unusable replies and provider failures separately. Read the wrong answers.

example.title: Where the minus sign sits matters

graph.accessibilityLabel: Graph of minus (x minus 1) squared on [−1, 1]. The curve lies above the dashed chord joining (−1, −4) and (1, 0).
Graph of (x minus 1) squared on [−1, 1]. The curve lies below the dashed chord joining (−1, 4) and (1, 0).

example.explanation: The first squares the term, then negates it. The second negates the term, then squares it.
example.caption: Examples on [−1, 1]. These are not measured model errors.

evidence.title: The evidence so far
evidence.description: All labels were correct in four reviewed frontier-model confirmation runs. Some exploratory runs with older or non-frontier models had errors. We have not established a frontier-model limitation.

slides.title: What does the score tell us?
slides.scoreDefinition: Macro-F1 averages the F1 scores for convex, concave, and neither. A higher value means better classification on the tested tasks.

highScore.title: High score: verify these three things

examples.title: All three classes are handled well
examples.description: Check that recall is high for convex, concave, and neither.

examples.title: The interval is used correctly
examples.description: Check answers to tasks that depend on the interval’s endpoints.

examples.title: The expression is read correctly
examples.description: Check explanations for correct use of parentheses and minus signs.

lowScore.title: Low score: check these three causes

examples.title: One class is often missed
examples.description: Check whether the model keeps choosing the same label.

examples.title: The expression or interval is misread
examples.description: Look for a missed restriction or a misplaced minus sign.

examples.title: The reply cannot be scored as a label
examples.description: Check for invalid JSON or a reply cut short by its output limit.

slides.closing:
Read the answers, per-class recall, and variation across trials.
A high score alone does not prove correct reasoning or reliable agent behavior.
